response.passage: Light behaves in predictable ways when it interacts with different materials. When light travels from one transparent medium to another, it changes speed, causing it to bend specifically at the boundary between the two media. This bending, known as refraction, occurs regardless of whether the medium is a liquid, gas, or solid. When we use lenses, the light rays do not stop at the image location; instead, they continue traveling through space, allowing us to see the image from different angles. A concave lens always produces a virtual, diminished image, regardless of the object's distance, because it diverges light rays. In contrast, the power of a lens is inversely proportional to its focal length, meaning a lens that bends light more sharply has a shorter focal length and higher power. Furthermore, when we look at a mirror, the image is not physically located on the glass surface itself, but appears to be behind it due to the reflection of light rays. Finally, magnification tells us about the image size and orientation; a negative magnification value indicates that the image is inverted, but it does not necessarily mean the image is smaller than the object.
response.summary: Light changes direction at the boundary of different media through refraction. Lenses and mirrors create images through the manipulation of light rays, where power relates to focal length and magnification indicates orientation.
